content: 1. The responsibility for managing an outbreak should be shared among multiple local, state, and federal agencies. The specific agencies involved will depend on the characteristics of the outbreak, such as the type of pathogen, the suspected or implicated source, the number of individuals affected, and the resources required to address the situation. 2. Outbreak response teams should have pre-established protocols for investigating outbreaks and access to resources that enable them to answer critical questions and make informed decisions during an outbreak. 3. A regularly updated list of individuals and organizations, both within and outside the agency, who should be contacted in the event of an outbreak, must be maintained. 4. Team members should receive training on the agency's outbreak response protocols and their specific roles within the team. Training can be delivered through classroom courses, self-study, team exercises, interagency drills, on-the-job training during real-life investigations, and debriefings after each outbreak investigation. 5. Health departments should assemble and familiarize themselves with the resources necessary for outbreak investigations before an outbreak occurs. These resources include support personnel for communication and data entry, legal counsel, equipment, supplies, outbreak investigation documents, and reference materials. 6. Agencies should establish procedures for routinely reviewing and replacing outdated or missing supplies, equipment, and reference materials as part of their outbreak response protocols. 7. A standardized process, including a data collection form, should be in place to receive complaints of potential foodborne illnesses from the public. Using an enteric illness log or database to track complaints and designating a specific individual to review all complaints can help identify patterns and potential outbreaks. 8. 9. 10. Policies for sharing information among members of the investigation team, their associated agencies, and implicated facilities should be established to facilitate communication during an outbreak. 11. Effective communication is critical during the investigation of a foodborne disease outbreak. Agencies should develop methods for communication with key individuals and organizations before an outbreak occurs. These include the outbreak investigation team, other local, state, and federal authorities, local organizations, the food industry, professional groups, the public, affected individuals and their families, and the media. 12. 13. Agencies should establish protocols for actions and outcomes required before an implicated facility or food source can resume normal operations. They should also develop methods to monitor these facilities. 14. Agencies should create a process for generating after-action reports following investigations. These reports should include lessons learned and action items for follow-up and quality improvement. 15. Legal preparedness is essential for an effective outbreak response. This includes having the necessary laws and legal authorities to support surveillance, detection, investigation, and control activities; ensuring professional staff are competent in using their legal authorities; establishing agreements for coordinated implementation of laws across jurisdictions and sectors; and having access to information on best practices for using legal tools in outbreak response. 16. If an outbreak affects multiple jurisdictions or exceeds the resources or expertise of a particular agency, investigators should escalate the investigation and involve other agencies as soon as the need is identified. 17. Local health department investigators should notify their state program, and state health department investigators should notify the CDC and the appropriate food-regulatory agency. 18. An Incident Command System (ICS) should be used to provide a structured framework for internal communication among primary responders, public information officers, and security and safety officers, as well as for external liaison with other entities. 19. Foodborne disease surveillance involves the routine monitoring of enteric diseases potentially transmitted through food. It serves multiple functions, including detecting disease clusters and identifying problems in food production or delivery. 20. Three general surveillance methods are used to detect foodborne disease outbreaks: pathogen-specific surveillance, notification/complaint systems, and syndromic surveillance. 21. In pathogen-specific surveillance, healthcare providers and laboratories report individual cases of disease to public health agencies when specific pathogens are identified in patient specimens or certain clinical syndromes are recognized (e.g., hemolytic uremic syndrome or botulism). Clinical laboratories also forward selected patient isolates or other clinical materials to public health laboratories. 22. Limitations of pathogen-specific surveillance include its reliance on routine testing and reporting to public health agencies, as well as delays in cluster detection and follow-up due to the time required for events to occur between patient infection and recognition as part of a cluster. 23. If the sensitivity of pathogen-specific surveillance is low, small outbreaks or those spread over time and space are more likely to be missed. Additionally, reported cases may differ significantly from unreported cases, leading to mischaracterization of an outbreak. 24. The prevalence of a disease in the community can make it more challenging to identify outbreaks of that disease and to distinguish background cases from outbreak cases. 25. Increasing the specificity of case definitions by including more detailed agent classifications (e.g., subtype results) or certain time, place, or person characteristics among cases can improve outbreak detection.
